title: Shloka 119
subtitle: Millions of Lakṣmīs, then a moon and a rainbow

namas.gloss: Served By Millions Of Lakṣmīs Made Her Handmaids
namas.translation: One sidelong look from her turns countless goddesses of fortune into attendants, and it is these who then wait on her.

commentary.meaning: The first line is a single name of sixteen syllables, one of the longest in the hymn, and it is built as a small machine: her sidelong glance turns ten million Lakṣmīs into handmaids, and it is those handmaids who then wait on her. The same glance both produces the servants and is the reason there are any. Since Lakṣmī is the goddess to whom the whole world addresses its requests for prosperity, saying that she exists in tens of millions and that all of them are in service is a way of settling a question of rank without argument. Then the verse changes scale completely. Having filled a whole line with a crowd, it turns inward and begins locating her in the body of the person reciting: at the crown of the head, where she is the colour of the moon, and at the forehead, where she is the arc of Indra's bow. The sequence does not stop at the end of the verse; the following one places her in the heart with the brightness of the sun. What begins as a court scene of unmanageable size ends as a set of coordinates on a human skull.
commentary.history:
Kaṭākṣa is the sidelong look, the glance thrown from the outer corner of the eye, and in the poetry of this tradition it is not a decorative gesture but the operative instrument. What she does, she does by looking; the literature is full of the claim that a single glance suffices for what nothing else can accomplish. The word is a compound of kaṭa, the temple or side of the head, and akṣa, the eye, so it means literally the eye turned to the side.

Kiṅkarī is worth pausing over. A kiṃkara is a servant, and the Sanskrit lexicographers derive the word transparently from the question kiṃ karomi, what shall I do — the attendant defined by standing ready and asking for instructions. The feminine kiṅkarī is the handmaid. The compound then says that the glance did not summon servants but converted them: kiṅkarībhūta, become-a-handmaid, with the abstract-forming suffix that turns a noun into a state something enters. They were goddesses of fortune, and after the look they are staff.

Kamalā is a name of Lakṣmī, from kamala, the lotus, on which she stands and which she holds. Lakṣmī is the object of the Śrī Sūkta, an early hymn appended to the Ṛgveda rather than belonging to its body, and of a very large part of the devotional practice of ordinary households, where she is petitioned for exactly what her name promises: gold, cattle, food, good fortune. Koṭi is ten million, and it is the standard Sanskrit hyperbole for a number too large to matter. Placing ten million of her in service is a theological claim made without any theological vocabulary, and it is the same claim the tradition makes when it calls its own vidyā the auspicious one, śrīvidyā, in the verse immediately preceding: prosperity is not the goal of this practice but a by-product it has in abundance.

With śiraḥsthitā the hymn moves to a different kind of statement. She is placed in the head — and the sequence that begins here runs through the brow to the heart in the following verse, each station given a light of its own. This is the vocabulary of the internal disciplines, in which the practitioner locates a deity at specified points in the body and holds attention there. The moon at the crown belongs to a standard scheme in which the cool lunar nectar is stored at the top of the head and the sun burns lower down; the Saundaryalaharī describes an ascent through the body that terminates in the thousand-petalled lotus at the crown, and the crown is where Śrīvidyā's internal yoga also ends. Candranibhā simply says her appearance is that of the moon, and the choice of comparison brings with it coolness and whiteness as much as brightness.

The rainbow at the forehead is harder to place. Indradhanus, Indra's bow, is the ordinary Sanskrit word for a rainbow, and behind it lies the Vedic image of the sky-god's weapon appearing in the storm. What a rainbow contributes that the moon does not is multiplicity: it is not one colour but a band of them, and prabhā, radiance, is here the radiance of something refracted. The hymn does not explain the choice, and it is worth resisting the temptation to force it into the tidy triad of moon, sun and fire that governs much of the surrounding literature — the brow simply gets a rainbow, and the meditation is asked to see a spectrum there rather than a single hue.

One textual matter deserves notice. The second line prints bhālasthendradhanuḥprabhā as a single word, because the final ā of bhālasthā and the initial i of indradhanuḥprabhā combine by ordinary sandhi into e. Two names are therefore concealed inside one written form. Divisions of this kind are where the count of exactly one thousand is decided, and different nāmāvalīs occasionally cut the text at different points; the reading followed here treats bhālasthā and indradhanuḥprabhā as separate names, which is the usual practice.
commentary.practice:
Sixteen syllables is a long time to be without a breath, and the first line of this verse is one name. Do not attempt it as a single sound. Break it where the meaning breaks: kaṭākṣa, the glance; kiṅkarī, handmaid; bhūta, become; kamalā, Lakṣmī; koṭi, ten million; sevitā, served by. Six pieces, learned as six, and then run together at speed. Reciters who try to memorise the syllables in order rather than the words in order almost always lose the middle of it.

The cluster ṅk in kiṅkarī is one of the few Sanskrit conjuncts an English speaker already owns: ṅ is the guttural nasal in sink and finger, made at the same place as k, and it is written with its own letter in Devanagari. The kṣ of kaṭākṣa is guttural k running straight into retroflex ṣ. Both ṭ sounds in the line, in kaṭākṣa and koṭi, are retroflex, made with the tongue tip curled back, and they are the same sound as in trikūṭā and kāmakoṭikā in the verse before.

The second line contains two visargas, and this verse is a good place to learn to say them. A visarga is a voiceless breath that carries a faint echo of the vowel before it, so śiraḥ ends with something like a whispered ha, and dhanuḥ with a whispered hu. In both places here the visarga stands before a voiceless consonant and is retained rather than transformed, which is why the printed text keeps it: śiraḥsthitā, indradhanuḥprabhā. Do not swallow them. A dropped visarga is the commonest single fault in recitation by learners, and the two in this line are exposed enough to be heard.

Sthi and sthā, in śiraḥsthitā and bhālasthā, are dental s followed by an aspirated dental th: the tongue stays at the teeth and there is a distinct puff of breath. In candranibhā the cluster ndra is three consonants — dental n, dental d, then r — and it recurs immediately in indradhanuḥ, so the line gives you the same difficulty twice within four syllables.

The archanā needs care here, because the written line hides a boundary. The offerings are kaṭākṣakiṅkarībhūtakamalākoṭisevitāyai, śiraḥsthitāyai, candranibhāyai, bhālasthāyai and indradhanuḥprabhāyai — five, not four. Anyone who learned the verse from the running text and never saw it divided will tend to offer bhālasthendradhanuḥprabhāyai as a single name and finish the thousand one short.

As for what the verse asks: the change of scale between its two lines is the whole of it. The first line is external, public and enormous, a throne room with ten million attendants in it. The second is interior, private and small, and it asks the reciter to put attention at the top of the head and then at the space between the brows and to find a particular quality of light at each. Reciting the two at the same speed and in the same tone flattens the verse. It is better to let the first line run and then slow, so that the shift from a crowd to a coordinate is audible.

crossReferences.translation: Golden of colour, tawny, wearing garlands of gold and silver, shining like the moon, made of gold — bring Lakṣmī to me, o knower of all that is born.
crossReferences.relevance: The hymn every Hindu household has some acquaintance with, and the standard address to the goddess of fortune. Setting it beside the first name of this verse shows what the name is doing: the deity whom the Vedic supplicant asks the fire to fetch is, here, present in tens of millions and employed as a maid. Note also that the Śrī Sūkta already calls her candrā, moon-like, the same comparison the sahasranāma will use two names later of Lalitā at the crown of the head.

crossReferences.deva: महीं मूलाधारे कमपि मणिपूरे हुतवहं स्थितं स्वाधिष्ठाने हृदि मरुतमाकाशमुपरि । मनोऽपि भ्रूमध्ये सकलमपि भित्त्वा कुलपथं सहस्रारे पद्मे सह रहसि पत्या विहरसे ॥
crossReferences.iast: mahīṃ mūlādhāre kam api maṇipūre hutavahaṃ sthitaṃ svādhiṣṭhāne hṛdi marutam ākāśam upari | mano 'pi bhrūmadhye sakalam api bhittvā kulapathaṃ sahasrāre padme saha rahasi patyā viharase ||
crossReferences.translation: Piercing earth in the root-support, water in the jewelled city, the fire that stands in her own dwelling, wind in the heart, space above that, and mind too in the middle of the brows — piercing the whole path of the family, you take your pleasure with your husband, alone with him, in the thousand-petalled lotus.
crossReferences.relevance: The classical description of the ascent that the names of this verse presuppose, and the reason the crown of the head is where the sequence starts. Two details are worth noticing. The middle of the brows, bhrūmadhya, is the station the sahasranāma calls bhāla. And the poem's assignment of the elements is not the one most later handbooks give, since it puts water at the navel centre and fire at the one below it; the schemes in this literature are less standardised than summaries of them suggest.

references.title: Hindu Goddesses: Visions of the Divine Feminine in the Hindu Religious Tradition
references.author: David R. Kinsley (University of California Press, 1986)
references.note: The chapter on Lakṣmī is the efficient way to find out who is being demoted in the first name of this verse — her Vedic background, the Śrī Sūkta, the association with kingship and with the churning of the ocean. Kinsley writes plainly and does not inflate his material.

references.title: Auspicious Wisdom: The Texts and Traditions of Śrīvidyā Śākta Tantrism in South India
references.author: Douglas Renfrew Brooks (SUNY Press, 1992)
references.note: For the internal geography the second line assumes. Brooks describes the placements a practitioner performs, the centres in the body and the way a deity is installed at each, with enough ritual detail to show that śiraḥsthitā and bhālasthā are instructions rather than descriptions.

references.title: Kuṇḍalinī: The Energy of the Depths
references.author: Lilian Silburn, tr. Jacques Gontier (SUNY Press, 1988)
references.note: A careful study of the internal yoga in the nondual Śaiva sources, useful here because Silburn works from texts rather than from the popularised diagrams and is explicit about where the traditions disagree with one another about the number and placement of the centres.

references.title: Śrī Lalitā Sahasranāma Stotram
references.author: M. S. Subbulakshmi (recorded for HMV; widely reissued and streamed)
references.note: The recording most people in South India have heard, and a reasonable model for pace and for the placement of the caesura. Two cautions: she recites the stotra continuously rather than as the nāmāvalī, so the name-boundary hidden inside bhālasthendradhanuḥprabhā is not audible; and her tempo is faster than a beginner should attempt.
